milestone.title: AT&T enters the general-purpose computer business with its Unix-based 3B line
milestone.note: The newly divested telephone giant's March 27 market entry put Bell Labs' Unix and AT&T-designed 32-bit hardware into direct commercial competition with IBM, DEC, Data General, Wang and Hewlett-Packard.

lead.headline: AT&T Throws Down a Unix Gauntlet With Six 3B Computers
lead.dek: The post-divestiture giant puts Unix System V and its own 32-bit architecture at the center of a sweeping commercial challenge.
body: AT&T formally entered the general-purpose computer business on March 27, opening a campaign that reaches from a desktop multi-user machine to fault-tolerant systems. Only months after the Bell System divestiture, the company is carrying Bell Labs software and AT&T-designed processors into direct competition with IBM, DEC, Data General, Wang and Hewlett-Packard.

Six announced models make up the 3B family, and every one runs AT&T Unix System V. The desktop 3B2 uses a 32-bit architecture, comes with 256K of memory and can serve as many as 18 users or work as a single-user machine. The larger 3B5 employs AT&T’s WE 32000 microprocessor, with versions intended for roughly 30 or 60 users.

At the upper end, the 3B20D emphasizes fault tolerance for banking, reservation and military work. AT&T says more than 1,200 related 3B20S systems are already operating inside its own companies, giving the sales pitch a substantial in-house proving ground.

The opening route is deliberately commercial: value-added resellers and customers able to provide applications come first, joined by 3B Net and a PC Interface. AT&T says 800 sales and technical people have been trained and plans a 6,000-person sales force by year’s end, while Olivetti handles European marketing.

The line’s first public showing is scheduled for COMDEX Winter in Los Angeles, April 5-7. Hardware sales are only part of the stakes: if the 3B family wins converts, Unix System V could move from a respected technical foundation toward the broad industry standard AT&T plainly wants it to become.

stories.headline: Police Raids Put Britain’s Games-Cassette Pirates Under Pressure
body: Police and Trading Standards raids reported in Salford and Hull have put unusually concrete numbers on the commercial counterfeiting trade. Ocean Software director David Ward estimated that a Salford warehouse held about 20,000 cassettes with a retail value near £100,000; police valued the blank media at £9,500.

Named copies included current games such as Jet Set Willy, Atic-Atac, Bugaboo and Harrier Attack. A separate Hull seizure recovered 150 cassettes after a tip from Software Projects. The actions target bulk sellers under deception and trade-description law, not home users, and charges in Hull had not yet been brought at press time.

stories.headline: IBM Rations PCs and XTs as the Component Squeeze Bites
body: IBM has limited dealers to 25 PC and XT machines a month and is quoting delivery four weeks after orders, a striking restriction for the market’s fastest-growing personal-computer standard. The shortage reaches Intel 8088 processors, 64K RAM chips and TTL components.

The squeeze lands only two weeks after IBM announced 20 percent price cuts. A licensing agreement with Intel and pilot U.S. production of the 8088 point toward relief, but for now dealers must ration machines just as lower prices promise to stimulate demand.

stories.headline: Sinclair Microdrives Reach London Shops
body: Forty long-awaited Sinclair Microdrives reached Computers of Wigmore Street, where six sold within half an hour. The miniature cartridge drive costs £49.95, or £79.95 with Interface 1; blank cartridges are £4.95.

Sinclair expects to send 20,000 Microdrive and Interface 1 units into shops each month. After delays severe enough to create a black market in order forms, an ordinary retail sale is news in itself, though full QL production is still taking time.

stories.headline: Macintosh Commands the West Coast Computer Faire
body: Apple gave away one Macintosh each day at the ninth West Coast Computer Faire in San Francisco, where the compact new machine drew the show’s liveliest attention. Elsewhere, IBM PC software dominated and exhibitors increasingly bundled “wordware” with programs.

The floor offered little major new hardware, but falling storage prices stood out: Electro Mavin advertised a 20MB eight-inch Winchester drive for the equivalent of about £1,100. A closing seminar on “The Personal Computing Backlash” captured an industry wondering what remains after the home-computer price war.

undergroundDesk.headline: Cassette Raids Put Counterfeiters on Notice
undergroundDesk.dek: Police and trading officers seize alleged copies of current British micro hits.
body: A warehouse raid in Salford reportedly uncovered about 20,000 games cassettes, while a separate Hull action seized 150 more after a tip from Software Projects. The named titles range from Jet Set Willy and Atic-Atac to Bugaboo and Harrier Attack.

The cases show publishers and authorities turning from warnings to enforcement as the games market grows. The report concerns commercial counterfeiting and legal action; it offers no copying instructions.
